author: Jesus Baltazar
title: EPISD weighs buyouts for upper administration amid looming budget shortfall - NewsBreak
text:
By Jesus Baltazar No media credit provided. ,
1 hours ago
EL PASO, Texas ( KTSM ) — The El Paso Independent School District (EPISD) is considering early retirement buyouts for senior central office staff as the district braces for a massive budget shortfall next school year.
The district placed an item on the board meeting agenda for Tuesday, April 21, to discuss a proposed financial incentive for central office employees who announce their departure early.
If approved, the 2026 Resign/Retire Early Notification Incentive Program would offer a $3,000 payout to all full-time central office personnel who submit written notice of their intent to resign or retire by May 8, 2026.
Teacher union representatives told KTSM 9 News this push for efficiency comes as the district faces a steep budget shortfall for the upcoming school year, after initially expecting to adopt a balanced budget.
El Paso ISD launches bond steering committee to look at future Ross Moore of the El Paso AFT and Norma De La Rosa of the El Paso Teachers Association said they learned from district staff that EPISD could face anywhere from a $5 million to $20 million deficit. This is due to a sudden recalculation by the Texas Education Agency (TEA), leaving districts statewide with less relief for revenue lost to the state’s new homestead tax exemptions.
“It is late in the budget cycle for this surprise, and one major Texas school district is dealing with a $180,000,000 deficit. I have not heard of any progress in getting the state to make things right as of yesterday,“ Moore said.
Moore said that initially, the state promised EPISD $21.5 million in “hold harmless” funding to make up for local property tax revenue lost to the state’s new $140,000 homestead tax exemption.
Texas voters approve historic property tax cuts However, he said the TEA recently revised its calculations, slashing that relief down to just $3.7 million, with the state now only covering revenue losses tied to frozen levies for seniors and disabled homeowners, forcing the district to absorb the rest of the impact.
“There will be less money coming in from (senior or disabled) taxpayers (into the district) because of the homestead exemption,” De La Rosa said. “When that was passed through the legislature, we asked how would we, as a district, be able to recoup that money? And the word that we got back from the state was that districts would be held harmless, with the understanding that the difference would be made up by the state with state funding. What we’re finding out is that there is a very strong possibility of the state reneging on that, which is why there may be a bigger deficit than was anticipated.”
During a board meeting on Tuesday, April 14, district staff from the Finance Committee made a budget development presentation to the board, highlighting the district’s administrative staffing structure and cost ratio.
Notably, the presentation revealed that EPISD currently employs 76 administrators at the director level or higher. That is nearly double the amount at neighboring Socorro ISD (36) and Ysleta ISD (41), despite all three districts serving a similar number of students.
“We are heavier on the upper-level positions from director and up,” EPISD Superintendent Brian Lusk said during the meeting. “As we look at this chart, we are significantly heavy on multiple levels and we will need to really realign our positions as a district to get to where we need to be as an organization so that the work that’s happening is happening closer to the campus.”
El Paso sees over 4K school voucher applications; public, private educators weigh in on what it means Expressing their full support for the proposed buyouts, both Moore and De La Rosa applauded the district for prioritizing cost-saving measures at the upper administrative levels rather than affecting personnel who work directly with students.
“This is going to be politically messy as pockets of power and privilege are challenged,” Moore said. “This is also necessary and long overdue. Juan Cabrera and his band of miscreants doubled the number of directors and above during his tenure. Had he not done so, EPISD would be between 35 to 40 directors and above, on par with SISD and YISD. And, who knows how much of the savings could have gone to your classrooms?”
“Prior to Dr. Lusk arriving, we were just seeing more and more people being moved into central offices with positions that were basically very redundant,” Norma De La Rosa, President of the El Paso Teachers Association, said. “You may have five people doing exactly the same job.”
Board President Leah Hanany emphasized that the district’s priority is to keep financial cuts away from students.
“This is an effort to show the community that we’re not going to be looking at classroom cuts first,” Hanany said. “We’re going to be evaluating, especially as we’re rightsizing our district, evaluating our budget with the understanding that central office and upper administration also has to be taken into consideration.”
